q.t: The Bill of Rights of 1689 confirmed which of these?
q.e: The Bill of Rights, 1689, confirmed the rights of Parliament and the limits of the king's power. Parliament took control of who could be monarch and declared that the king or queen must be a Protestant. Every year the monarch had to ask Parliament to renew funding for the army and the navy.
o: That the king or queen must be a Protestant
That the monarch could raise taxes without Parliament
That the monarch could appoint judges freely
That Parliament would meet only when the king summoned it

q.t: After the Bill of Rights, how often did a new Parliament have to be elected?
q.e: A new Parliament had to be elected at least every three years. Later this became seven years and now it is five years.

q.t: Which TWO groups were the main political groupings in Parliament after the Glorious Revolution?
q.e: There were two main groups in Parliament, known as the Whigs and the Tories. The modern Conservative Party is still sometimes referred to as the Tories. This was the beginning of party politics.

q.t: What happened from 1695 that was important for the development of a free press?
q.e: This was also an important time for the development of a free press, newspapers and other publications which are not controlled by the government. From 1695, newspapers were allowed to operate without a government licence.
o: Newspapers were allowed to operate without a government licence
The first newspaper in England was printed
The government began to fund newspapers
Newspapers were required to be balanced by law

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Some constituencies were controlled by a single wealthy family. These were called 'pocket boroughs'. Other constituencies had hardly any voters and were called 'rotten boroughs'.
o: A constituency controlled by a single wealthy family was called a pocket borough
A constituency controlled by a single wealthy family was called a rotten borough

q.t: Which refugees came to Britain from France between 1680 and 1720?
q.e: Between 1680 and 1720 many refugees called Huguenots came from France. They were Protestants and had been persecuted for their religion. Many were educated and skilled and worked as scientists, in banking, or in weaving or other crafts.

q.t: The Act of Union of 1707 created which kingdom?
q.e: The Act of Union, known as the Treaty of Union in Scotland, was agreed in 1707, creating the Kingdom of Great Britain. Although Scotland was no longer an independent country, it kept its own legal and education systems and Presbyterian Church.
o: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
The Kingdom of England and Wales

q.t: Which TWO things did Scotland keep after the Act of Union of 1707?
q.e: Although Scotland was no longer an independent country, it kept its own legal and education systems and Presbyterian Church.

q.t: Why did Parliament choose George I to be king in 1714?
q.e: When Queen Anne died in 1714, Parliament chose a German, George I, to be the next king, because he was Anne's nearest Protestant relative. George I did not speak very good English and this increased his need to rely on his ministers.
o: He was Anne's nearest Protestant relative
He had won a war against France
He was elected by the people

q.t: Who was the first man to be called Prime Minister, and in which years did he serve?
q.e: The most important minister in Parliament became known as the Prime Minister. The first man to be called this was Sir Robert Walpole, who was Prime Minister from 1721 to 1742.
o: The Duke of Wellington, from 1721 to 1742

q.t: At which battle was Bonnie Prince Charlie defeated in 1746?
q.e: In 1745 there was another attempt to put a Stuart king back on the throne. Charles Edward Stuart, Bonnie Prince Charlie, the grandson of James II, landed in Scotland. He was defeated by George II's army at the Battle of Culloden in 1746.

q.t: What were the 'Highland Clearances'?
q.e: Many Scottish landlords destroyed individual small farms, known as 'crofts', to make space for large flocks of sheep and cattle. Evictions became very common in the early 19th century. Many Scottish people left for North America at this time.
o: Small farms were destroyed to make space for sheep and cattle
Highland forests were cleared for shipbuilding
Clan chieftains were exiled to France
Castles in the Highlands were demolished

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Robert Burns wrote only in standard English.
q.e: Known in Scotland as 'The Bard', Robert Burns was a Scottish poet. He wrote in the Scots language, English with some Scottish words, and standard English. His best-known work is probably the song Auld Lang Syne.

q.t: Which song by Robert Burns is sung when people celebrate the New Year?
q.e: Burns' best-known work is probably the song Auld Lang Syne, which is sung by people in the UK and other countries when they are celebrating the New Year, or Hogmanay as it is called in Scotland.
o: I Vow to Thee, My Country

q.t: Which TWO Scottish thinkers of the Enlightenment are named in the handbook?
q.e: Many of the great thinkers of the Enlightenment were Scottish. Adam Smith developed ideas about economics which are still referred to today. David Hume's ideas about human nature continue to influence philosophers.

q.t: What is one of the most important principles of the Enlightenment, according to the handbook?
q.e: One of the most important principles of the Enlightenment was that everyone should have the right to their own political and religious beliefs and that the state should not try to dictate to them. This continues to be an important principle in the UK today.
o: Everyone should have the right to their own political and religious beliefs
The state should control religious worship
Only property owners should have political rights
Science should be kept separate from philosophy

q.t: How long does giving blood take, according to the handbook?
q.e: Donated blood is used by hospitals to help people with a wide range of injuries and illnesses. Giving blood only takes about an hour to do.

q.t: Which organ can living people donate?
q.e: Many people in the UK are waiting for organ transplants. If you register to be an organ donor, it can make it easier for your family to decide whether to donate your organs when you die. Living people can also donate a kidney.

q.t: At what age can a person become a school governor, and is there an upper age limit?
q.e: School governors, or members of the school board in Scotland, must be aged 18 or over at the date of their election or appointment. There is no upper age limit.
o: 18 or over, with no upper age limit
18 or over, up to the age of 70
21 or over, with no upper age limit
16 or over, up to the age of 70

q.t: Which TWO are key roles of school governors, according to the handbook?
q.e: Governors and school boards have three key roles: setting the strategic direction of the school, ensuring accountability, and monitoring and evaluating school performance.
o: Setting the strategic direction of the school
Teaching lessons when staff are absent

q.t: What is 'canvassing'?
q.e: Political parties are particularly busy at election times. Members work hard to persuade people to vote for their candidates, for instance by handing out leaflets in the street or by knocking on people's doors and asking for their support. This is called 'canvassing'.
o: Asking people for their support, for example by knocking on doors
Counting the votes after an election
Registering to vote at your local council
Standing as a candidate for Parliament

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
You have to tell a canvasser how you intend to vote.
q.e: Members work hard to persuade people to vote for their candidates. This is called 'canvassing'. You don't have to tell a canvasser how you intend to vote if you don't want to.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: It is important to recycle as much of your waste as you can. Using recycled materials to make new products uses less energy. It also means that less rubbish is created, so the amount being put into landfill is reduced.
o: Recycling uses less energy and puts less rubbish into landfill
Recycling uses more energy and puts more rubbish into landfill

q.t: Which TWO of these does the handbook suggest as ways to look after the environment?
q.e: A good way to support your local community is to shop for products locally where you can. Walking and using public transport to get around when you can is also a good way to protect the environment. It means that you create less pollution than when you use a car.
o: Use a car for every journey
